./FAQ.md:31:
./FAQ.md:32:<h3 name="config">
./FAQ.md:33:Does ripgrep support configuration files?
./FAQ.md:34:</h3>
./FAQ.md:35:
./FAQ.md:36:Yes. See the
./FAQ.md:37:[guide's section on configuration files](GUIDE.md#configuration-file).
./FAQ.md:38:
./FAQ.md:39:
./FAQ.md:40:<h3 name="changelog">
./FAQ.md:41:What's changed in ripgrep recently?
./FAQ.md:42:</h3>
./FAQ.md:43:
./FAQ.md:44:Please consult ripgrep's [CHANGELOG](CHANGELOG.md).
./FAQ.md:45:
./FAQ.md:46:
./FAQ.md:47:<h3 name="release">
./FAQ.md:48:When is the next release?
./FAQ.md:49:</h3>
./FAQ.md:50:
./FAQ.md:51:ripgrep is a project whose contributors are volunteers. A release schedule
./FAQ.md:52:adds undue stress to said volunteers. Therefore, releases are made on a best
./FAQ.md:53:effort basis and no dates **will ever be given**.
./FAQ.md:54:
./FAQ.md:55:An exception to this _can be_ high impact bugs. If a ripgrep release contains
./FAQ.md:56:a significant regression, then there will generally be a strong push to get a
./FAQ.md:57:patch release out with a fix. However, no promises are made.
./FAQ.md:58:
./FAQ.md:59:
./FAQ.md:60:<h3 name="manpage">
./FAQ.md:61:Does ripgrep have a man page?
./FAQ.md:62:</h3>
./FAQ.md:63:
./FAQ.md:64:Yes. If you installed ripgrep through a package manager on a Unix system, then
./FAQ.md:65:it would have ideally been installed for you in the proper location. In which
./FAQ.md:66:case, `man rg` should just work.
./FAQ.md:67:
./FAQ.md:68:Otherwise, you can ask ripgrep to generate the man page:
./FAQ.md:69:
./FAQ.md:70:```
./FAQ.md:71:$ mkdir -p man/man1
./FAQ.md:72:$ rg --generate man > man/man1/rg.1
./FAQ.md:73:$ MANPATH="$PWD/man" man rg
./FAQ.md:74:```
./FAQ.md:75:
./FAQ.md:76:Or, if your version of `man` supports the `-l/--local-file` flag, then this
./FAQ.md:77:will suffice:
./FAQ.md:78:
./FAQ.md:79:```
./FAQ.md:80:$ rg --generate man | man -l -
./FAQ.md:81:```
./FAQ.md:82:
./FAQ.md:83:Note that the man page's documentation for options is equivalent to the output
./FAQ.md:84:shown in `rg --help`. To see more condensed documentation (one line per flag),
./FAQ.md:85:run `rg -h`.
./FAQ.md:86:
./FAQ.md:87:The man page is also included in all
./FAQ.md:88:[ripgrep binary releases](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/releases).
./FAQ.md:89:
./FAQ.md:90:
./FAQ.md:91:<h3 name="complete">
./FAQ.md:92:Does ripgrep have support for shell auto-completion?
./FAQ.md:93:</h3>
./FAQ.md:94:
./FAQ.md:95:Yes! If you installed ripgrep through a package manager on a Unix system, then
./FAQ.md:96:the shell completion files included in the release archive should have been
./FAQ.md:97:installed for you automatically. If not, you can generate completions using
./FAQ.md:98:ripgrep's command line interface.
./FAQ.md:99:
./FAQ.md:100:For **bash**:
./FAQ.md:101:
./FAQ.md:102:```
./FAQ.md:103:$ dir="$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/bash_completion"
./FAQ.md:104:$ mkdir -p "$dir"
./FAQ.md:105:$ rg --generate complete-bash > "$dir/rg.bash"
./FAQ.md:106:```
./FAQ.md:107:
./FAQ.md:108:For **fish**:
./FAQ.md:109:
./FAQ.md:110:```
./FAQ.md:111:$ dir="$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fish/completions"
./FAQ.md:112:$ mkdir -p "$dir"
./FAQ.md:113:$ rg --generate complete-fish > "$dir/rg.fish"
./FAQ.md:114:```
./FAQ.md:115:
./FAQ.md:116:For **zsh**, the recommended approach is:
./FAQ.md:117:
./FAQ.md:118:```zsh
./FAQ.md:119:$ dir="$HOME/.zsh-complete"
./FAQ.md:120:$ mkdir -p "$dir"
./FAQ.md:121:$ rg --generate complete-zsh > "$dir/_rg"
./FAQ.md:122:```
./FAQ.md:123:
./FAQ.md:124:And then add `$HOME/.zsh-complete` to your `fpath` in, e.g., your
./FAQ.md:125:`$HOME/.zshrc` file:
./FAQ.md:126:
./FAQ.md:127:```zsh
./FAQ.md:128:fpath=($HOME/.zsh-complete $fpath)
./FAQ.md:129:```
./FAQ.md:130:
./FAQ.md:131:Or if you'd prefer to load and generate completions at the same time, you can
./FAQ.md:132:add the following to your `$HOME/.zshrc` file:
./FAQ.md:133:
./FAQ.md:134:```zsh
./FAQ.md:135:$ source <(rg --generate complete-zsh)
./FAQ.md:136:```
./FAQ.md:137:
./FAQ.md:138:Note though that while this approach is easier to setup, is generally slower
./FAQ.md:139:than the previous method, and will add more time to loading your shell prompt.
./FAQ.md:140:
./FAQ.md:141:For **PowerShell**, create the completions:
./FAQ.md:142:
./FAQ.md:143:```
./FAQ.md:144:$ rg --generate complete-powershell > _rg.ps1
./FAQ.md:145:```
./FAQ.md:146:
./FAQ.md:147:And then add `. _rg.ps1` to your PowerShell
./FAQ.md:148:[profile](https://technet.microsoft.com/en-us/library/bb613488(v=vs.85).aspx)
./FAQ.md:149:(note the leading period). If the `_rg.ps1` file is not on your `PATH`, do
./FAQ.md:150:`. /path/to/_rg.ps1` instead.
./FAQ.md:151:
./FAQ.md:152:
./FAQ.md:153:<h3 name="order">
./FAQ.md:154:How can I get results in a consistent order?
./FAQ.md:155:</h3>
./FAQ.md:156:
./FAQ.md:157:By default, ripgrep uses parallelism to execute its search because this makes
./FAQ.md:158:the search much faster on most modern systems. This in turn means that ripgrep
./FAQ.md:159:has a non-deterministic aspect to it, since the interleaving of threads during
./FAQ.md:160:the execution of the program is itself non-deterministic. This has the effect
./FAQ.md:161:of printing results in a somewhat arbitrary order, and this order can change
./FAQ.md:162:from run to run of ripgrep.
./FAQ.md:163:
./FAQ.md:164:The only way to make the order of results consistent is to ask ripgrep to
./FAQ.md:165:sort the output. Currently, this will disable all parallelism. (On smaller
./FAQ.md:166:repositories, you might not notice much of a performance difference!) You
./FAQ.md:167:can achieve this with the `--sort path` flag.
./FAQ.md:168:
./FAQ.md:169:There is more discussion on this topic here:
./FAQ.md:170:https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/issues/152
./FAQ.md:171:
./FAQ.md:172:
./FAQ.md:173:<h3 name="encoding">
./FAQ.md:174:How do I search files that aren't UTF-8?
./FAQ.md:175:</h3>
./FAQ.md:176:
./FAQ.md:177:See the [guide's section on file encoding](GUIDE.md#file-encoding).
./FAQ.md:178:
./FAQ.md:179:
./FAQ.md:180:<h3 name="compressed">
./FAQ.md:181:How do I search compressed files?
./FAQ.md:182:</h3>
./FAQ.md:183:
./FAQ.md:184:ripgrep's `-z/--search-zip` flag will cause it to search compressed files
./FAQ.md:185:automatically. Currently, this supports gzip, bzip2, xz, lzma, lz4, Brotli and
./FAQ.md:186:Zstd. Each of these requires the corresponding `gzip`, `bzip2`, `xz`,
./FAQ.md:187:`lz4`, `brotli` and `zstd` binaries to be installed on your system. (That is,
./FAQ.md:188:ripgrep does decompression by shelling out to another process.)
./FAQ.md:189:
./FAQ.md:190:ripgrep currently does not search archive formats, so `*.tar.gz` files, for
./FAQ.md:191:example, are skipped.
./FAQ.md:192:
./FAQ.md:193:
./FAQ.md:194:<h3 name="multiline">
./FAQ.md:195:How do I search over multiple lines?
./FAQ.md:196:</h3>
./FAQ.md:197:
./FAQ.md:198:The `-U/--multiline` flag enables ripgrep to report results that span over
./FAQ.md:199:multiple lines.
./FAQ.md:200:
./FAQ.md:201:
./FAQ.md:202:<h3 name="fancy">
./FAQ.md:203:How do I use lookaround and/or backreferences?
./FAQ.md:204:</h3>
./FAQ.md:205:
./FAQ.md:206:ripgrep's default regex engine does not support lookaround or backreferences.
./FAQ.md:207:This is primarily because the default regex engine is implemented using finite
./FAQ.md:208:state machines in order to guarantee a linear worst case time complexity on all
./FAQ.md:209:inputs. Backreferences are not possible to implement in this paradigm, and
./FAQ.md:210:lookaround appears difficult to do efficiently.
./FAQ.md:211:
./FAQ.md:212:However, ripgrep optionally supports using PCRE2 as the regex engine instead of
./FAQ.md:213:the default one based on finite state machines. You can enable PCRE2 with the
./FAQ.md:214:`-P/--pcre2` flag. For example, in the root of the ripgrep repo, you can easily
./FAQ.md:215:find all palindromes:
./FAQ.md:216:
./FAQ.md:217:```
./FAQ.md:218:$ rg -P '(\w{10})\1'
./FAQ.md:219:tests/misc.rs
./FAQ.md:220:483:    cmd.arg("--max-filesize").arg("44444444444444444444");
./FAQ.md:221:globset/src/glob.rs
./FAQ.md:222:1206:    matches!(match7, "a*a*a*a*a*a*a*a*a", "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa");
./FAQ.md:223:```
./FAQ.md:224:
./FAQ.md:225:If your version of ripgrep doesn't support PCRE2, then you'll get an error
./FAQ.md:226:message when you try to use the `-P/--pcre2` flag:
./FAQ.md:227:
./FAQ.md:228:```
./FAQ.md:229:$ rg -P '(\w{10})\1'
./FAQ.md:230:PCRE2 is not available in this build of ripgrep
./FAQ.md:231:```
./FAQ.md:232:
./FAQ.md:233:Most of the releases distributed by the ripgrep project here on GitHub will
./FAQ.md:234:come bundled with PCRE2 enabled. If you installed ripgrep through a different
./FAQ.md:235:means (like your system's package manager), then please reach out to the
./FAQ.md:236:maintainer of that package to see whether it's possible to enable the PCRE2
./FAQ.md:237:feature.
./FAQ.md:238:
./FAQ.md:239:
./FAQ.md:240:<h3 name="colors">
./FAQ.md:241:How do I configure ripgrep's colors?
./FAQ.md:242:</h3>
./FAQ.md:243:
./FAQ.md:244:ripgrep has two flags related to colors:
./FAQ.md:245:
./FAQ.md:246:* `--color` controls *when* to use colors.
./FAQ.md:247:* `--colors` controls *which* colors to use.
./FAQ.md:248:
./FAQ.md:249:The `--color` flag accepts one of the following possible values: `never`,
./FAQ.md:250:`auto`, `always` or `ansi`. The `auto` value is the default and will cause
./FAQ.md:251:ripgrep to only enable colors when it is printing to a terminal. But if you
./FAQ.md:252:pipe ripgrep to a file or some other process, then it will suppress colors.
./FAQ.md:253:
./FAQ.md:254:The `--colors` flag is a bit more complicated. The general format is:
./FAQ.md:255:
./FAQ.md:256:```
./FAQ.md:257:--colors '{type}:{attribute}:{value}'
./FAQ.md:258:```
./FAQ.md:259:
./FAQ.md:260:* `{type}` should be one of `path`, `line`, `column` or `match`. Each of these
./FAQ.md:261:  correspond to the four different types of things that ripgrep will add color
./FAQ.md:262:  to in its output. Select the type whose color you want to change.
./FAQ.md:263:* `{attribute}` should be one of `fg`, `bg` or `style`, corresponding to
./FAQ.md:264:  foreground color, background color, or miscellaneous styling (such as whether
./FAQ.md:265:  to bold the output or not).
./FAQ.md:266:* `{value}` is determined by the value of `{attribute}`. If
./FAQ.md:267:  `{attribute}` is `style`, then `{value}` should be one of `nobold`,
./FAQ.md:268:  `bold`, `nointense`, `intense`, `nounderline`, `underline`, `noitalic` or
./FAQ.md:269:  `italic`. If `{attribute}` is `fg` or `bg`, then `{value}` should be a color.
./FAQ.md:270:
./FAQ.md:271:A color is specified by either one of eight of English names, a single 256-bit
./FAQ.md:272:number or an RGB triple (with over 16 million possible values, or "true
./FAQ.md:273:color").
./FAQ.md:274:
./FAQ.md:275:The color names are `red`, `blue`, `green`, `cyan`, `magenta`, `yellow`,
./FAQ.md:276:`white` or `black`.
./FAQ.md:277:
./FAQ.md:278:A single 256-bit number is a value in the range 0-255 (inclusive). It can
./FAQ.md:279:either be in decimal format (e.g., `62`) or hexadecimal format (e.g., `0x3E`).
./FAQ.md:280:
./FAQ.md:281:An RGB triple corresponds to three numbers (decimal or hexadecimal) separated
./FAQ.md:282:by commas.
./FAQ.md:283:
./FAQ.md:284:As a special case, `--colors '{type}:none'` will clear all colors and styles
./FAQ.md:285:associated with `{type}`, which lets you start with a clean slate (instead of
./FAQ.md:286:building on top of ripgrep's default color settings).
./FAQ.md:287:
./FAQ.md:288:Here's an example that highlights the matches with a nice blue background with
./FAQ.md:289:bolded white text:
./FAQ.md:290:
./FAQ.md:291:```
./FAQ.md:292:$ rg somepattern \
./FAQ.md:293:    --colors 'match:none' \
./FAQ.md:294:    --colors 'match:bg:0x33,0x66,0xFF' \
./FAQ.md:295:    --colors 'match:fg:white' \
./FAQ.md:296:    --colors 'match:style:bold'
./FAQ.md:297:```
./FAQ.md:298:
./FAQ.md:299:Colors are an ideal candidate to set in your
./FAQ.md:300:[configuration file](GUIDE.md#configuration-file). See the
./FAQ.md:301:[question on emulating The Silver Searcher's output style](#silver-searcher-output)
./FAQ.md:302:for an example specific to colors.
./FAQ.md:303:
./FAQ.md:304:
./FAQ.md:305:<h3 name="truecolors-windows">
./FAQ.md:306:How do I enable true colors on Windows?
./FAQ.md:307:</h3>
./FAQ.md:308:
./FAQ.md:309:First, see the previous question's
./FAQ.md:310:[answer on configuring colors](#colors).
./FAQ.md:311:
./FAQ.md:312:Secondly, coloring on Windows is a bit complicated. If you're using a terminal
./FAQ.md:313:like Cygwin, then it's likely true color support already works out of the box.
./FAQ.md:314:However, if you are using a normal Windows console (`cmd` or `PowerShell`) and
./FAQ.md:315:a version of Windows prior to 10, then there is no known way to get true
./FAQ.md:316:color support. If you are on Windows 10 and using a Windows console, then
./FAQ.md:317:true colors should work out of the box with one caveat: you might need to
./FAQ.md:318:clear ripgrep's default color settings first. That is, instead of this:
./FAQ.md:319:
./FAQ.md:320:```
./FAQ.md:321:$ rg somepattern --colors 'match:fg:0x33,0x66,0xFF'
./FAQ.md:322:```
./FAQ.md:323:
./FAQ.md:324:you should do this
./FAQ.md:325:
./FAQ.md:326:```
./FAQ.md:327:$ rg somepattern --colors 'match:none' --colors 'match:fg:0x33,0x66,0xFF'
./FAQ.md:328:```
./FAQ.md:329:
./FAQ.md:330:This is because ripgrep might set the default style for `match` to `bold`, and
./FAQ.md:331:it seems like Windows 10's VT100 support doesn't permit bold and true color
./FAQ.md:332:ANSI escapes to be used simultaneously. The work-around above will clear
./FAQ.md:333:ripgrep's default styling, allowing you to craft it exactly as desired.
./FAQ.md:334:
./FAQ.md:335:
./FAQ.md:336:<h3 name="stop-ripgrep">
./FAQ.md:337:How do I stop ripgrep from messing up colors when I kill it?
./FAQ.md:338:</h3>
./FAQ.md:339:
./FAQ.md:340:Type in `color` in cmd.exe (Command Prompt) and `echo -ne "\033[0m"` on
./FAQ.md:341:Unix-like systems to restore your original foreground color.
./FAQ.md:342:
./FAQ.md:343:In PowerShell, you can add the following code to your profile which will
./FAQ.md:344:restore the original foreground color when `Reset-ForegroundColor` is called.
./FAQ.md:345:Including the `Set-Alias` line will allow you to call it with simply `color`.
./FAQ.md:346:
./FAQ.md:347:```powershell
./FAQ.md:348:$OrigFgColor = $Host.UI.RawUI.ForegroundColor
./FAQ.md:349:function Reset-ForegroundColor {
./FAQ.md:350:	$Host.UI.RawUI.ForegroundColor = $OrigFgColor
./FAQ.md:351:}
./FAQ.md:352:Set-Alias -Name color -Value Reset-ForegroundColor
./FAQ.md:353:```
./FAQ.md:354:
./FAQ.md:355:PR [#187](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/pull/187) fixed this, and it
./FAQ.md:356:was later deprecated in
./FAQ.md:357:[#281](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/issues/281). A full explanation is
./FAQ.md:358:available
./FAQ.md:359:[here](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/issues/281#issuecomment-269093893).
./FAQ.md:360:
./FAQ.md:361:
./FAQ.md:362:<h3 name="because-cygwin">
./FAQ.md:363:Why does using a leading `/` on Windows fail?
./FAQ.md:364:</h3>
./FAQ.md:365:
./FAQ.md:366:If you're using cygwin on Windows and try to search for a pattern beginning
./FAQ.md:367:with a `/`, then it's possible that cygwin is mangling that pattern without
./FAQ.md:368:your knowledge. For example, if you tried running `rg /foo` in a cygwin shell
./FAQ.md:369:on Windows, then cygwin might mistakenly perform path translation on `/foo`,
./FAQ.md:370:which would result in `rg C:/msys64/foo` being searched instead.
./FAQ.md:371:
./FAQ.md:372:You can fix this in one of three ways:
./FAQ.md:373:
./FAQ.md:374:1. Stop using cygwin.
./FAQ.md:375:2. Escape the leading slash with an additional slash. e.g., `rg //foo`.
./FAQ.md:376:3. Temporarily disable path translation by setting `MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1`. e.g.,
./FAQ.md:377:   `MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 rg /foo`.
./FAQ.md:378:
./FAQ.md:379:For more details, see https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/issues/1277
./FAQ.md:380:
./FAQ.md:381:
./FAQ.md:382:<h3 name="size-limit">
./FAQ.md:383:How do I get around the regex size limit?
./FAQ.md:384:</h3>
./FAQ.md:385:
./FAQ.md:386:If you've given ripgrep a particularly large pattern (or a large number of
./FAQ.md:387:smaller patterns), then it is possible that it will fail to compile because it
./FAQ.md:388:hit a pre-set limit. For example:
./FAQ.md:389:
./FAQ.md:390:```
./FAQ.md:391:$ rg '\pL{1000}'
./FAQ.md:392:Compiled regex exceeds size limit of 10485760 bytes.
./FAQ.md:393:```
./FAQ.md:394:
./FAQ.md:395:(Note: `\pL{1000}` may look small, but `\pL` is the character class containing
./FAQ.md:396:all Unicode letters, which is quite large. *And* it's repeated 1000 times.)
./FAQ.md:397:
./FAQ.md:398:In this case, you can work around by simply increasing the limit:
./FAQ.md:399:
./FAQ.md:400:```
./FAQ.md:401:$ rg '\pL{1000}' --regex-size-limit 1G
./FAQ.md:402:```
./FAQ.md:403:
./FAQ.md:404:Increasing the limit to 1GB does not necessarily mean that ripgrep will use
./FAQ.md:405:that much memory. The limit just says that it's allowed to (approximately) use
./FAQ.md:406:that much memory for constructing the regular expression.
./FAQ.md:407:
./FAQ.md:408:
./FAQ.md:409:<h3 name="dfa-size">
./FAQ.md:410:How do I make the <code>-f/--file</code> flag faster?
./FAQ.md:411:</h3>
./FAQ.md:412:
./FAQ.md:413:The `-f/--file` permits one to give a file to ripgrep which contains a pattern
./FAQ.md:414:on each line. ripgrep will then report any line that matches any of the
./FAQ.md:415:patterns.
./FAQ.md:416:
./FAQ.md:417:If this pattern file gets too big, then it is possible ripgrep will slow down
./FAQ.md:418:dramatically. *Typically* this is because an internal cache is too small, and
./FAQ.md:419:will cause ripgrep to spill over to a slower but more robust regular expression
./FAQ.md:420:engine. If this is indeed the problem, then it is possible to increase this
./FAQ.md:421:cache and regain speed. The cache can be controlled via the `--dfa-size-limit`
./FAQ.md:422:flag. For example, using `--dfa-size-limit 1G` will set the cache size to 1GB.
./FAQ.md:423:(Note that this doesn't mean ripgrep will use 1GB of memory automatically, but
./FAQ.md:424:it will allow the regex engine to if it needs to.)
./FAQ.md:425:
./FAQ.md:426:
./FAQ.md:427:<h3 name="silver-searcher-output">
./FAQ.md:428:How do I make the output look like The Silver Searcher's output?
./FAQ.md:429:</h3>
./FAQ.md:430:
./FAQ.md:431:Use the `--colors` flag, like so:
./FAQ.md:432:
./FAQ.md:433:```
./FAQ.md:434:rg --colors line:fg:yellow      \
./FAQ.md:435:   --colors line:style:bold     \
./FAQ.md:436:   --colors path:fg:green       \
./FAQ.md:437:   --colors path:style:bold     \
./FAQ.md:438:   --colors match:fg:black      \
./FAQ.md:439:   --colors match:bg:yellow     \
./FAQ.md:440:   --colors match:style:nobold  \
./FAQ.md:441:   foo
./FAQ.md:442:```
./FAQ.md:443:
./FAQ.md:444:Alternatively, add your color configuration to your ripgrep config file (which
./FAQ.md:445:is activated by setting the `RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH` environment variable to point
./FAQ.md:446:to your config file). For example:
./FAQ.md:447:
./FAQ.md:448:```
./FAQ.md:449:$ cat $HOME/.config/ripgrep/rc
./FAQ.md:450:--colors=line:fg:yellow
./FAQ.md:451:--colors=line:style:bold
./FAQ.md:452:--colors=path:fg:green
./FAQ.md:453:--colors=path:style:bold
./FAQ.md:454:--colors=match:fg:black
./FAQ.md:455:--colors=match:bg:yellow
./FAQ.md:456:--colors=match:style:nobold
./FAQ.md:457:$ RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH=$HOME/.config/ripgrep/rc rg foo
./FAQ.md:458:```
./FAQ.md:459:
./FAQ.md:460:
./FAQ.md:461:<h3 name="pcre2-slow">
./FAQ.md:462:Why does ripgrep get slower when I enable PCRE2 regexes?
./FAQ.md:463:</h3>
./FAQ.md:464:
./FAQ.md:465:When you use the `--pcre2` (`-P` for short) flag, ripgrep will use the PCRE2
./FAQ.md:466:regex engine instead of the default. Both regex engines are quite fast,
./FAQ.md:467:but PCRE2 provides a number of additional features such as look-around and
./FAQ.md:468:backreferences that many enjoy using. This is largely because PCRE2 uses
./FAQ.md:469:a backtracking implementation where as the default regex engine uses a finite
./FAQ.md:470:automaton based implementation. The former provides the ability to add lots of
./FAQ.md:471:bells and whistles over the latter, but the latter executes with worst case
./FAQ.md:472:linear time complexity.
./FAQ.md:473:
./FAQ.md:474:With that out of the way, if you've used `-P` with ripgrep, you may have
./FAQ.md:475:noticed that it can be slower. The reasons for why this is are quite complex,
./FAQ.md:476:and they are complex because the optimizations that ripgrep uses to implement
./FAQ.md:477:fast search are complex.
./FAQ.md:478:
./FAQ.md:479:The task ripgrep has before it is somewhat simple; all it needs to do is search
./FAQ.md:480:a file for occurrences of some pattern and then print the lines containing
./FAQ.md:481:those occurrences. The problem lies in what is considered a valid match and how
./FAQ.md:482:exactly we read the bytes from a file.
./FAQ.md:483:
./FAQ.md:484:In terms of what is considered a valid match, remember that ripgrep will only
./FAQ.md:485:report matches spanning a single line by default. The problem here is that
./FAQ.md:486:some patterns can match across multiple lines, and ripgrep needs to prevent
./FAQ.md:487:that from happening. For example, `foo\sbar` will match `foo\nbar`. The most
./FAQ.md:488:obvious way to achieve this is to read the data from a file, and then apply
./FAQ.md:489:the pattern search to that data for each line. The problem with this approach
./FAQ.md:490:is that it can be quite slow; it would be much faster to let the pattern
./FAQ.md:491:search across as much data as possible. It's faster because it gets rid of the
./FAQ.md:492:overhead of finding the boundaries of every line, and also because it gets rid
./FAQ.md:493:of the overhead of starting and stopping the pattern search for every single
./FAQ.md:494:line. (This is operating under the general assumption that matching lines are
./FAQ.md:495:much rarer than non-matching lines.)
./FAQ.md:496:
./FAQ.md:497:It turns out that we can use the faster approach by applying a very simple
./FAQ.md:498:restriction to the pattern: *statically prevent* the pattern from matching
./FAQ.md:499:through a `\n` character. Namely, when given a pattern like `foo\sbar`,
./FAQ.md:500:ripgrep will remove `\n` from the `\s` character class automatically. In some
./FAQ.md:501:cases, a simple removal is not so easy. For example, ripgrep will return an
./FAQ.md:502:error when your pattern includes a `\n` literal:
./FAQ.md:503:
./FAQ.md:504:```
./FAQ.md:505:$ rg '\n'
./FAQ.md:506:the literal '"\n"' is not allowed in a regex
./FAQ.md:507:```
./FAQ.md:508:
./FAQ.md:509:So what does this have to do with PCRE2? Well, ripgrep's default regex engine
./FAQ.md:510:exposes APIs for doing syntactic analysis on the pattern in a way that makes
./FAQ.md:511:it quite easy to strip `\n` from the pattern (or otherwise detect it and report
./FAQ.md:512:an error if stripping isn't possible). PCRE2 seemingly does not provide a
./FAQ.md:513:similar API, so ripgrep does not do any stripping when PCRE2 is enabled. This
./FAQ.md:514:forces ripgrep to use the "slow" search strategy of searching each line
./FAQ.md:515:individually.
./FAQ.md:516:
./FAQ.md:517:OK, so if enabling PCRE2 slows down the default method of searching because it
./FAQ.md:518:forces matches to be limited to a single line, then why is PCRE2 also sometimes
./FAQ.md:519:slower when performing multiline searches? Well, that's because there are
./FAQ.md:520:*multiple* reasons why using PCRE2 in ripgrep can be slower than the default
./FAQ.md:521:regex engine. This time, blame PCRE2's Unicode support, which ripgrep enables
./FAQ.md:522:by default. In particular, PCRE2 cannot simultaneously enable Unicode support
./FAQ.md:523:and search arbitrary data. That is, when PCRE2's Unicode support is enabled,
./FAQ.md:524:the data **must** be valid UTF-8 (to do otherwise is to invoke undefined
./FAQ.md:525:behavior). This is in contrast to ripgrep's default regex engine, which can
./FAQ.md:526:enable Unicode support and still search arbitrary data. ripgrep's default
./FAQ.md:527:regex engine simply won't match invalid UTF-8 for a pattern that can otherwise
./FAQ.md:528:only match valid UTF-8. Why doesn't PCRE2 do the same? This author isn't
./FAQ.md:529:familiar with its internals, so we can't comment on it here.
./FAQ.md:530:
./FAQ.md:531:The bottom line here is that we can't enable PCRE2's Unicode support without
./FAQ.md:532:simultaneously incurring a performance penalty for ensuring that we are
./FAQ.md:533:searching valid UTF-8. In particular, ripgrep will transcode the contents
./FAQ.md:534:of each file to UTF-8 while replacing invalid UTF-8 data with the Unicode
./FAQ.md:535:replacement codepoint. ripgrep then disables PCRE2's own internal UTF-8
./FAQ.md:536:checking, since we've guaranteed the data we hand it will be valid UTF-8. The
./FAQ.md:537:reason why ripgrep takes this approach is because if we do hand PCRE2 invalid
./FAQ.md:538:UTF-8, then it will report a match error if it comes across an invalid UTF-8
./FAQ.md:539:sequence. This is not good news for ripgrep, since it will stop it from
./FAQ.md:540:searching the rest of the file, and will also print potentially undesirable
./FAQ.md:541:error messages to users.
./FAQ.md:542:
./FAQ.md:543:All right, the above is a lot of information to swallow if you aren't already
./FAQ.md:544:familiar with ripgrep internals. Let's make this concrete with some examples.
./FAQ.md:545:First, let's get some data big enough to magnify the performance differences:
./FAQ.md:546:
./FAQ.md:547:```
./FAQ.md:548:$ curl -O 'https://burntsushi.net/stuff/subtitles2016-sample.gz'
./FAQ.md:549:$ gzip -d subtitles2016-sample
./FAQ.md:550:$ md5sum subtitles2016-sample
./FAQ.md:551:e3cb796a20bbc602fbfd6bb43bda45f5   subtitles2016-sample
./FAQ.md:552:```
./FAQ.md:553:
./FAQ.md:554:To search this data, we will use the pattern `^\w{42}$`, which contains exactly
./FAQ.md:555:one hit in the file and has no literals. Having no literals is important,
./FAQ.md:556:because it ensures that the regex engine won't use literal optimizations to
./FAQ.md:557:speed up the search. In other words, it lets us reason coherently about the
./FAQ.md:558:actual task that the regex engine is performing.
./FAQ.md:559:
./FAQ.md:560:Let's now walk through a few examples in light of the information above. First,
./FAQ.md:561:let's consider the default search using ripgrep's default regex engine and
./FAQ.md:562:then the same search with PCRE2:
./FAQ.md:563:
./FAQ.md:564:```
./FAQ.md:565:$ time rg '^\w{42}$' subtitles2016-sample
./FAQ.md:566:21225780:EverymajordevelopmentinthehistoryofAmerica
./FAQ.md:567:
./FAQ.md:568:real    0m1.783s
./FAQ.md:569:user    0m1.731s
./FAQ.md:570:sys     0m0.051s
./FAQ.md:571:
./FAQ.md:572:$ time rg -P '^\w{42}$' subtitles2016-sample
./FAQ.md:573:21225780:EverymajordevelopmentinthehistoryofAmerica
./FAQ.md:574:
./FAQ.md:575:real    0m2.458s
./FAQ.md:576:user    0m2.419s
./FAQ.md:577:sys     0m0.038s
./FAQ.md:578:```
./FAQ.md:579:
./FAQ.md:580:In this particular example, both pattern searches are using a Unicode aware
./FAQ.md:581:`\w` character class and both are counting lines in order to report line
./FAQ.md:582:numbers. The key difference here is that the first search will not search
./FAQ.md:583:line by line, but the second one will. We can observe which strategy ripgrep
./FAQ.md:584:uses by passing the `--trace` flag:
./FAQ.md:585:
./FAQ.md:586:```
./FAQ.md:587:$ rg '^\w{42}$' subtitles2016-sample --trace
./FAQ.md:588:[... snip ...]
./FAQ.md:589:TRACE|grep_searcher::searcher|grep-searcher/src/searcher/mod.rs:622: Some("subtitles2016-sample"): searching via memory map
./FAQ.md:590:TRACE|grep_searcher::searcher|grep-searcher/src/searcher/mod.rs:712: slice reader: searching via slice-by-line strategy
./FAQ.md:591:TRACE|grep_searcher::searcher::core|grep-searcher/src/searcher/core.rs:61: searcher core: will use fast line searcher
./FAQ.md:592:[... snip ...]
./FAQ.md:593:
./FAQ.md:594:$ rg -P '^\w{42}$' subtitles2016-sample --trace
./FAQ.md:595:[... snip ...]
./FAQ.md:596:TRACE|grep_searcher::searcher|grep-searcher/src/searcher/mod.rs:622: Some("subtitles2016-sample"): searching via memory map
./FAQ.md:597:TRACE|grep_searcher::searcher|grep-searcher/src/searcher/mod.rs:705: slice reader: needs transcoding, using generic reader
./FAQ.md:598:TRACE|grep_searcher::searcher|grep-searcher/src/searcher/mod.rs:685: generic reader: searching via roll buffer strategy
./FAQ.md:599:TRACE|grep_searcher::searcher::core|grep-searcher/src/searcher/core.rs:63: searcher core: will use slow line searcher
./FAQ.md:600:[... snip ...]
./FAQ.md:601:```
./FAQ.md:602:
./FAQ.md:603:The first says it is using the "fast line searcher" where as the latter says
./FAQ.md:604:it is using the "slow line searcher." The latter also shows that we are
./FAQ.md:605:decoding the contents of the file, which also impacts performance.
./FAQ.md:606:
./FAQ.md:607:Interestingly, in this case, the pattern does not match a `\n` and the file
./FAQ.md:608:we're searching is valid UTF-8, so neither the slow line-by-line search
./FAQ.md:609:strategy nor the decoding are necessary. We could fix the former issue with
./FAQ.md:610:better PCRE2 introspection APIs. We can actually fix the latter issue with
./FAQ.md:611:ripgrep's `--no-encoding` flag, which prevents the automatic UTF-8 decoding,
./FAQ.md:612:but will enable PCRE2's own UTF-8 validity checking. Unfortunately, it's slower
./FAQ.md:613:in my build of ripgrep:
./FAQ.md:614:
./FAQ.md:615:```
./FAQ.md:616:$ time rg -P '^\w{42}$' subtitles2016-sample --no-encoding
./FAQ.md:617:21225780:EverymajordevelopmentinthehistoryofAmerica
./FAQ.md:618:
./FAQ.md:619:real    0m3.074s
./FAQ.md:620:user    0m3.021s
./FAQ.md:621:sys     0m0.051s
./FAQ.md:622:```
./FAQ.md:623:
./FAQ.md:624:(Tip: use the `--trace` flag to verify that no decoding in ripgrep is
./FAQ.md:625:happening.)
./FAQ.md:626:
./FAQ.md:627:A possible reason why PCRE2's UTF-8 checking is slower is because it might
./FAQ.md:628:not be better than the highly optimized UTF-8 checking routines found in the
./FAQ.md:629:[`encoding_rs`](https://github.com/hsivonen/encoding_rs) library, which is what
./FAQ.md:630:ripgrep uses for UTF-8 decoding. Moreover, my build of ripgrep enables
./FAQ.md:631:`encoding_rs`'s SIMD optimizations, which may be in play here.
./FAQ.md:632:
./FAQ.md:633:Also, note that using the `--no-encoding` flag can cause PCRE2 to report
./FAQ.md:634:invalid UTF-8 errors, which causes ripgrep to stop searching the file:
./FAQ.md:635:
./FAQ.md:636:```
./FAQ.md:637:$ cat invalid-utf8
./FAQ.md:638:foobar
./FAQ.md:639:
./FAQ.md:640:$ xxd invalid-utf8
./FAQ.md:641:00000000: 666f 6fff 6261 720a                      foo.bar.
./FAQ.md:642:
./FAQ.md:643:$ rg foo invalid-utf8
./FAQ.md:644:1:foobar
./FAQ.md:645:
./FAQ.md:646:$ rg -P foo invalid-utf8
./FAQ.md:647:1:foo�bar
./FAQ.md:648:
./FAQ.md:649:$ rg -P foo invalid-utf8 --no-encoding
./FAQ.md:650:invalid-utf8: PCRE2: error matching: UTF-8 error: illegal byte (0xfe or 0xff)
./FAQ.md:651:```
./FAQ.md:652:
./FAQ.md:653:All right, so at this point, you might think that we could remove the penalty
./FAQ.md:654:for line-by-line searching by enabling multiline search. After all, our
./FAQ.md:655:particular pattern can't match across multiple lines anyway, so we'll still get
./FAQ.md:656:the results we want. Let's try it:
./FAQ.md:657:
./FAQ.md:658:```
./FAQ.md:659:$ time rg -U '^\w{42}$' subtitles2016-sample
./FAQ.md:660:21225780:EverymajordevelopmentinthehistoryofAmerica
./FAQ.md:661:
./FAQ.md:662:real    0m1.803s
./FAQ.md:663:user    0m1.748s
./FAQ.md:664:sys     0m0.054s
./FAQ.md:665:
./FAQ.md:666:$ time rg -P -U '^\w{42}$' subtitles2016-sample
./FAQ.md:667:21225780:EverymajordevelopmentinthehistoryofAmerica
./FAQ.md:668:
./FAQ.md:669:real    0m2.962s
./FAQ.md:670:user    0m2.246s
./FAQ.md:671:sys     0m0.713s
./FAQ.md:672:```
./FAQ.md:673:
./FAQ.md:674:Search times remain the same with the default regex engine, but the PCRE2
./FAQ.md:675:search gets _slower_. What happened? The secrets can be revealed with the
./FAQ.md:676:`--trace` flag once again. In the former case, ripgrep actually detects that
./FAQ.md:677:the pattern can't match across multiple lines, and so will fall back to the
./FAQ.md:678:"fast line search" strategy as with our search without `-U`.
./FAQ.md:679:
./FAQ.md:680:However, for PCRE2, things are much worse. Namely, since Unicode mode is still
./FAQ.md:681:enabled, ripgrep is still going to decode UTF-8 to ensure that it hands only
./FAQ.md:682:valid UTF-8 to PCRE2. Unfortunately, one key downside of multiline search is
./FAQ.md:683:that ripgrep cannot do it incrementally. Since matches can be arbitrarily long,
./FAQ.md:684:ripgrep actually needs the entire file in memory at once. Normally, we can use
./FAQ.md:685:a memory map for this, but because we need to UTF-8 decode the file before
./FAQ.md:686:searching it, ripgrep winds up reading the entire contents of the file on to
./FAQ.md:687:the heap before executing a search. Owch.
./FAQ.md:688:
./FAQ.md:689:OK, so Unicode is killing us here. The file we're searching is _mostly_ ASCII,
./FAQ.md:690:so maybe we're OK with missing some data. (Try `rg '[\w--\p{ascii}]'` to see
./FAQ.md:691:non-ASCII word characters that an ASCII-only `\w` character class would miss.)
./FAQ.md:692:We can disable Unicode in both searches, but this is done differently depending
./FAQ.md:693:on the regex engine we use:
./FAQ.md:694:
./FAQ.md:695:```
./FAQ.md:696:$ time rg '(?-u)^\w{42}$' subtitles2016-sample
./FAQ.md:697:21225780:EverymajordevelopmentinthehistoryofAmerica
./FAQ.md:698:
./FAQ.md:699:real    0m1.714s
./FAQ.md:700:user    0m1.669s
./FAQ.md:701:sys     0m0.044s
./FAQ.md:702:
./FAQ.md:703:$ time rg -P '^\w{42}$' subtitles2016-sample --no-pcre2-unicode
./FAQ.md:704:21225780:EverymajordevelopmentinthehistoryofAmerica
./FAQ.md:705:
./FAQ.md:706:real    0m1.997s
./FAQ.md:707:user    0m1.958s
./FAQ.md:708:sys     0m0.037s
./FAQ.md:709:```
./FAQ.md:710:
./FAQ.md:711:For the most part, ripgrep's default regex engine performs about the same.
./FAQ.md:712:PCRE2 does improve a little bit, and is now almost as fast as the default
./FAQ.md:713:regex engine. If you look at the output of `--trace`, you'll see that ripgrep
./FAQ.md:714:will no longer perform UTF-8 decoding, but it does still use the slow
./FAQ.md:715:line-by-line searcher.
./FAQ.md:716:
./FAQ.md:717:At this point, we can combine all of our insights above: let's try to get off
./FAQ.md:718:of the slow line-by-line searcher by enabling multiline mode, and let's stop
./FAQ.md:719:UTF-8 decoding by disabling Unicode support:
./FAQ.md:720:
./FAQ.md:721:```
./FAQ.md:722:$ time rg -U '(?-u)^\w{42}$' subtitles2016-sample
./FAQ.md:723:21225780:EverymajordevelopmentinthehistoryofAmerica
./FAQ.md:724:
./FAQ.md:725:real    0m1.714s
./FAQ.md:726:user    0m1.655s
./FAQ.md:727:sys     0m0.058s
./FAQ.md:728:
./FAQ.md:729:$ time rg -P -U '^\w{42}$' subtitles2016-sample --no-pcre2-unicode
./FAQ.md:730:21225780:EverymajordevelopmentinthehistoryofAmerica
./FAQ.md:731:
./FAQ.md:732:real    0m1.121s
./FAQ.md:733:user    0m1.071s
./FAQ.md:734:sys     0m0.048s
./FAQ.md:735:```
./FAQ.md:736:
./FAQ.md:737:Ah, there's PCRE2's JIT shining! ripgrep's default regex engine once again
./FAQ.md:738:remains about the same, but PCRE2 no longer needs to search line-by-line and it
./FAQ.md:739:no longer needs to do any kind of UTF-8 checks. This allows the file to get
./FAQ.md:740:memory mapped and passed right through PCRE2's JIT at impressive speeds. (As
./FAQ.md:741:a brief and interesting historical note, the configuration of "memory map +
./FAQ.md:742:multiline + no-Unicode" is exactly the configuration used by The Silver
./FAQ.md:743:Searcher. This analysis perhaps sheds some reasoning as to why that
./FAQ.md:744:configuration is useful!)
./FAQ.md:745:
./FAQ.md:746:In summary, if you want PCRE2 to go as fast as possible and you don't care
./FAQ.md:747:about Unicode and you don't care about matches possibly spanning across
./FAQ.md:748:multiple lines, then enable multiline mode with `-U` and disable PCRE2's
./FAQ.md:749:Unicode support with the `--no-pcre2-unicode` flag.
./FAQ.md:750:
./FAQ.md:751:Caveat emptor: This author is not a PCRE2 expert, so there may be APIs that can
./FAQ.md:752:improve performance that the author missed. Similarly, there may be alternative
./FAQ.md:753:designs for a searching tool that are more amenable to how PCRE2 works.
./FAQ.md:754:
./FAQ.md:755:
./FAQ.md:756:<h3 name="rg-other-cmd">
./FAQ.md:757:When I run <code>rg</code>, why does it execute some other command?
./FAQ.md:758:</h3>
./FAQ.md:759:
./FAQ.md:760:It's likely that you have a shell alias or even another tool called `rg` which
./FAQ.md:761:is interfering with ripgrep. Run `which rg` to see what it is.
./FAQ.md:762:
./FAQ.md:763:(Notably, the Rails plug-in for
./FAQ.md:764:[Oh My Zsh](https://github.com/robbyrussell/oh-my-zsh/wiki/Plugins#rails) sets
./FAQ.md:765:up an `rg` alias for `rails generate`.)
./FAQ.md:766:
./FAQ.md:767:Problems like this can be resolved in one of several ways:
./FAQ.md:768:
./FAQ.md:769:* If you're using the OMZ Rails plug-in, disable it by editing the `plugins`
./FAQ.md:770:  array in your zsh configuration.
./FAQ.md:771:* Temporarily bypass an existing `rg` alias by calling ripgrep as
./FAQ.md:772:  `command rg`, `\rg`, or `'rg'`.
./FAQ.md:773:* Temporarily bypass an existing alias or another tool named `rg` by calling
./FAQ.md:774:  ripgrep by its full path (e.g., `/usr/bin/rg` or `/usr/local/bin/rg`).
./FAQ.md:775:* Permanently disable an existing `rg` alias by adding `unalias rg` to the
./FAQ.md:776:  bottom of your shell configuration file (e.g., `.bash_profile` or `.zshrc`).
./FAQ.md:777:* Give ripgrep its own alias that doesn't conflict with other tools/aliases by
./FAQ.md:778:  adding a line like the following to the bottom of your shell configuration
./FAQ.md:779:  file: `alias ripgrep='command rg'`.
./FAQ.md:780:
./FAQ.md:781:
./FAQ.md:782:<h3 name="rg-alias-windows">
./FAQ.md:783:How do I create an alias for ripgrep on Windows?
./FAQ.md:784:</h3>
./FAQ.md:785:
./FAQ.md:786:Often you can find a need to make alias for commands you use a lot that set
./FAQ.md:787:certain flags. But PowerShell function aliases do not behave like your typical
./FAQ.md:788:linux shell alias. You always need to propagate arguments and `stdin` input.
./FAQ.md:789:But it cannot be done simply as
./FAQ.md:790:`function grep() { $input | rg.exe --hidden $args }`
./FAQ.md:791:
./FAQ.md:792:Use below example as reference to how setup alias in PowerShell.
./FAQ.md:793:
./FAQ.md:794:```powershell
./FAQ.md:795:function grep {
./FAQ.md:796:    $count = @($input).Count
./FAQ.md:797:    $input.Reset()
./FAQ.md:798:
./FAQ.md:799:    if ($count) {
./FAQ.md:800:        $input | rg.exe --hidden $args
./FAQ.md:801:    }
./FAQ.md:802:    else {
./FAQ.md:803:        rg.exe --hidden $args
./FAQ.md:804:    }
./FAQ.md:805:}
./FAQ.md:806:```
./FAQ.md:807:
./FAQ.md:808:PowerShell special variables:
./FAQ.md:809:
./FAQ.md:810:* input - is powershell `stdin` object that allows you to access its content.
./FAQ.md:811:* args - is array of arguments passed to this function.
./FAQ.md:812:
./FAQ.md:813:This alias checks whether there is `stdin` input and propagates only if there
./FAQ.md:814:is some lines. Otherwise empty `$input` will make powershell to trigger `rg` to
./FAQ.md:815:search empty `stdin`.
./FAQ.md:816:
./FAQ.md:817:
./FAQ.md:818:<h3 name="powershell-profile">
./FAQ.md:819:How do I create a PowerShell profile?
./FAQ.md:820:</h3>
./FAQ.md:821:
./FAQ.md:822:To customize powershell on start-up, there is a special PowerShell script that
./FAQ.md:823:has to be created. In order to find its location, type `$profile`.
./FAQ.md:824:See
./FAQ.md:825:[Microsoft's documentation](https://technet.microsoft.com/en-us/library/bb613488(v=vs.85).aspx)
./FAQ.md:826:for more details.
./FAQ.md:827:
./FAQ.md:828:Any PowerShell code in this file gets evaluated at the start of console. This
./FAQ.md:829:way you can have own aliases to be created at start.
./FAQ.md:830:
./FAQ.md:831:
./FAQ.md:832:<h3 name="pipe-non-ascii-windows">
./FAQ.md:833:How do I pipe non-ASCII content to ripgrep on Windows?
./FAQ.md:834:</h3>
./FAQ.md:835:
./FAQ.md:836:When piping input into native executables in PowerShell, the encoding of the
./FAQ.md:837:input is controlled by the `$OutputEncoding` variable. By default, this is set
./FAQ.md:838:to US-ASCII, and any characters in the pipeline that don't have encodings in
./FAQ.md:839:US-ASCII are converted to `?` (question mark) characters.
./FAQ.md:840:
./FAQ.md:841:To change this setting, set `$OutputEncoding` to a different encoding, as
./FAQ.md:842:represented by a .NET encoding object. Some common examples are below. The
./FAQ.md:843:value of this variable is reset when PowerShell restarts, so to make this
./FAQ.md:844:change take effect every time PowerShell is started add a line setting the
./FAQ.md:845:variable into your PowerShell profile.
./FAQ.md:846:
./FAQ.md:847:Example `$OutputEncoding` settings:
./FAQ.md:848:
./FAQ.md:849:* UTF-8 without BOM: `$OutputEncoding = [System.Text.UTF8Encoding]::new()`
./FAQ.md:850:* The console's output encoding:
./FAQ.md:851:  `$OutputEncoding = [System.Console]::OutputEncoding`
./FAQ.md:852:
./FAQ.md:853:If you continue to have encoding problems, you can also force the encoding
./FAQ.md:854:that the console will use for printing to UTF-8 with
./FAQ.md:855:`[System.Console]::OutputEncoding = [System.Text.Encoding]::UTF8`. This
./FAQ.md:856:will also reset when PowerShell is restarted, so you can add that line
./FAQ.md:857:to your profile as well if you want to make the setting permanent.
./FAQ.md:858:
./FAQ.md:859:<h3 name="search-and-replace">
./FAQ.md:860:How can I search and replace with ripgrep?
./FAQ.md:861:</h3>
./FAQ.md:862:
./FAQ.md:863:Using ripgrep alone, you can't. ripgrep is a search tool that will never
./FAQ.md:864:touch your files. However, the output of ripgrep can be piped to other tools
./FAQ.md:865:that do modify files on disk. See
./FAQ.md:866:[this issue](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/issues/74) for more
./FAQ.md:867:information.
./FAQ.md:868:
./FAQ.md:869:sed is one such tool that can modify files on disk. sed can take a filename
./FAQ.md:870:and a substitution command to search and replace in the specified file.
./FAQ.md:871:Files containing matching patterns can be provided to sed using
./FAQ.md:872:
./FAQ.md:873:```
./FAQ.md:874:rg foo --files-with-matches
./FAQ.md:875:```
./FAQ.md:876:
./FAQ.md:877:The output of this command is a list of filenames that contain a match for
./FAQ.md:878:the `foo` pattern.
./FAQ.md:879:
./FAQ.md:880:This list can be piped into `xargs`, which will split the filenames from
./FAQ.md:881:standard input into arguments for the command following xargs. You can use this
./FAQ.md:882:combination to pipe a list of filenames into sed for replacement. For example:
./FAQ.md:883:
./FAQ.md:884:```
./FAQ.md:885:rg foo --files-with-matches | xargs sed -i 's/foo/bar/g'
./FAQ.md:886:```
./FAQ.md:887:
./FAQ.md:888:will replace all instances of 'foo' with 'bar' in the files in which
./FAQ.md:889:ripgrep finds the foo pattern. The `-i` flag to sed indicates that you are
./FAQ.md:890:editing files in place, and `s/foo/bar/g` says that you are performing a
./FAQ.md:891:**s**ubstitution of the pattern `foo` for `bar`, and that you are doing this
./FAQ.md:892:substitution **g**lobally (all occurrences of the pattern in each file).
./FAQ.md:893:
./FAQ.md:894:Note: the above command assumes that you are using GNU sed. If you are using
./FAQ.md:895:BSD sed (the default on macOS and FreeBSD) then you must modify the above
./FAQ.md:896:command to be the following:
./FAQ.md:897:
./FAQ.md:898:```
./FAQ.md:899:rg foo --files-with-matches | xargs sed -i '' 's/foo/bar/g'
./FAQ.md:900:```
./FAQ.md:901:
./FAQ.md:902:The `-i` flag in BSD sed requires a file extension to be given to make backups
./FAQ.md:903:for all modified files. Specifying the empty string prevents file backups from
./FAQ.md:904:being made.
./FAQ.md:905:
./FAQ.md:906:Finally, if any of your file paths contain whitespace in them, then you might
./FAQ.md:907:need to delimit your file paths with a NUL terminator. This requires telling
./FAQ.md:908:ripgrep to output NUL bytes between each path, and telling xargs to read paths
./FAQ.md:909:delimited by NUL bytes:
./FAQ.md:910:
./FAQ.md:911:```
./FAQ.md:912:rg foo --files-with-matches -0 | xargs -0 sed -i 's/foo/bar/g'
./FAQ.md:913:```
./FAQ.md:914:
./FAQ.md:915:To learn more about sed, see the sed manual
./FAQ.md:916:[here](https://www.gnu.org/software/sed/manual/sed.html).
./FAQ.md:917:
./FAQ.md:918:Additionally, Facebook has a tool called
./FAQ.md:919:[fastmod](https://github.com/facebookincubator/fastmod)
./FAQ.md:920:that uses some of the same libraries as ripgrep and might provide a more
./FAQ.md:921:ergonomic search-and-replace experience.
./FAQ.md:922:
./FAQ.md:923:
./FAQ.md:924:<h3 name="license">
./FAQ.md:925:How is ripgrep licensed?
./FAQ.md:926:</h3>
./FAQ.md:927:
./FAQ.md:928:ripgrep is dual licensed under the
./FAQ.md:929:[Unlicense](https://unlicense.org/)
./FAQ.md:930:and MIT licenses. Specifically, you may use ripgrep under the terms of either
./FAQ.md:931:license.
./FAQ.md:932:
./FAQ.md:933:The reason why ripgrep is dual licensed this way is two-fold:
./FAQ.md:934:
./FAQ.md:935:1. I, as ripgrep's author, would like to participate in a small bit of
./FAQ.md:936:   ideological activism by promoting the Unlicense's goal: to disclaim
./FAQ.md:937:   copyright monopoly interest.
./FAQ.md:938:2. I, as ripgrep's author, would like as many people to use ripgrep as
./FAQ.md:939:   possible. Since the Unlicense is not a proven or well known license, ripgrep
./FAQ.md:940:   is also offered under the MIT license, which is ubiquitous and accepted by
./FAQ.md:941:   almost everyone.
./FAQ.md:942:
./FAQ.md:943:More specifically, ripgrep and all its dependencies are compatible with this
./FAQ.md:944:licensing choice. In particular, ripgrep's dependencies (direct and transitive)
./FAQ.md:945:will always be limited to permissive licenses. That is, ripgrep will never
./FAQ.md:946:depend on code that is not permissively licensed. This means rejecting any
./FAQ.md:947:dependency that uses a copyleft license such as the GPL, LGPL, MPL or any of
./FAQ.md:948:the Creative Commons ShareAlike licenses. Whether the license is "weak"
./FAQ.md:949:copyleft or not does not matter; ripgrep will **not** depend on it.
./FAQ.md:950:
./FAQ.md:951:
./FAQ.md:952:<h3 name="posix4ever">
./FAQ.md:953:Can ripgrep replace grep?
./FAQ.md:954:</h3>
./FAQ.md:955:
./FAQ.md:956:Yes and no.
./FAQ.md:957:
./FAQ.md:958:If, upon hearing that "ripgrep can replace grep," you *actually* hear, "ripgrep
./FAQ.md:959:can be used in every instance grep can be used, in exactly the same way, for
./FAQ.md:960:the same use cases, with exactly the same bug-for-bug behavior," then no,
./FAQ.md:961:ripgrep trivially *cannot* replace grep. Moreover, ripgrep will *never* replace
./FAQ.md:962:grep.
./FAQ.md:963:
./FAQ.md:964:If, upon hearing that "ripgrep can replace grep," you *actually* hear, "ripgrep
./FAQ.md:965:can replace grep in some cases and not in other use cases," then yes, that is
./FAQ.md:966:indeed true!
./FAQ.md:967:
./FAQ.md:968:Let's go over some of those use cases in favor of ripgrep. Some of these may
./FAQ.md:969:not apply to you. That's OK. There may be other use cases not listed here that
./FAQ.md:970:do apply to you. That's OK too.
./FAQ.md:971:
./FAQ.md:972:(For all claims related to performance in the following words, see my
./FAQ.md:973:[blog post](https://blog.burntsushi.net/ripgrep/)
./FAQ.md:974:introducing ripgrep.)
./FAQ.md:975:
./FAQ.md:976:* Are you frequently searching a repository of code? If so, ripgrep might be a
./FAQ.md:977:  good choice since there's likely a good chunk of your repository that you
./FAQ.md:978:  don't want to search. grep, can, of course, be made to filter files using
./FAQ.md:979:  recursive search, and if you don't mind writing out the requisite `--exclude`
./FAQ.md:980:  rules or writing wrapper scripts, then grep might be sufficient. (I'm not
./FAQ.md:981:  kidding, I myself did this with grep for almost a decade before writing
./FAQ.md:982:  ripgrep.) But if you instead enjoy having a search tool respect your
./FAQ.md:983:  `.gitignore`, then ripgrep might be perfect for you!
./FAQ.md:984:* Are you frequently searching non-ASCII text that is UTF-8 encoded? One of
./FAQ.md:985:  ripgrep's key features is that it can handle Unicode features in your
./FAQ.md:986:  patterns in a way that tends to be faster than GNU grep. Unicode features
./FAQ.md:987:  in ripgrep are enabled by default; there is no need to configure your locale
./FAQ.md:988:  settings to use ripgrep properly because ripgrep doesn't respect your locale
./FAQ.md:989:  settings.
./FAQ.md:990:* Do you need to search UTF-16 files and you don't want to bother explicitly
./FAQ.md:991:  transcoding them? Great. ripgrep does this for you automatically. No need
./FAQ.md:992:  to enable it.
./FAQ.md:993:* Do you need to search a large directory of large files? ripgrep uses
./FAQ.md:994:  parallelism by default, which tends to make it faster than a standard
./FAQ.md:995:  `grep -r` search. However, if you're OK writing the occasional
./FAQ.md:996:  `find ./ -print0 | xargs -P8 -0 grep` command, then maybe grep is good
./FAQ.md:997:  enough.
./FAQ.md:998:
./FAQ.md:999:Here are some cases where you might *not* want to use ripgrep. The same caveats
./FAQ.md:1000:for the previous section apply.
./FAQ.md:1001:
./FAQ.md:1002:* Are you writing portable shell scripts intended to work in a variety of
./FAQ.md:1003:  environments? Great, probably not a good idea to use ripgrep! ripgrep has
./FAQ.md:1004:  nowhere near the ubiquity of grep, so if you do use ripgrep, you might need
./FAQ.md:1005:  to futz with the installation process more than you would with grep.
./FAQ.md:1006:* Do you care about POSIX compatibility? If so, then you can't use ripgrep
./FAQ.md:1007:  because it never was, isn't and never will be POSIX compatible.
./FAQ.md:1008:* Do you hate tools that try to do something smart? If so, ripgrep is all about
./FAQ.md:1009:  being smart, so you might prefer to just stick with grep.
./FAQ.md:1010:* Is there a particular feature of grep you rely on that ripgrep either doesn't
./FAQ.md:1011:  have or never will have? If the former, file a bug report, maybe ripgrep can
./FAQ.md:1012:  do it! If the latter, well, then, just use grep.
./FAQ.md:1013:
./FAQ.md:1014:
./FAQ.md:1015:<h3 name="intentcountsforsomething">
./FAQ.md:1016:What does the "rip" in ripgrep mean?
./FAQ.md:1017:</h3>
./FAQ.md:1018:
./FAQ.md:1019:When I first started writing ripgrep, I called it `rep`, intending it to be a
./FAQ.md:1020:shorter variant of `grep`. Soon after, I renamed it to `xrep` since `rep`
./FAQ.md:1021:wasn't obvious enough of a name for my taste. And also because adding `x` to
./FAQ.md:1022:anything always makes it better, right?
./FAQ.md:1023:
./FAQ.md:1024:Before ripgrep's first public release, I decided that I didn't like `xrep`. I
./FAQ.md:1025:thought it was slightly awkward to type, and despite my previous praise of the
./FAQ.md:1026:letter `x`, I kind of thought it was pretty lame. Being someone who really
./FAQ.md:1027:likes Rust, I wanted to call it "rustgrep" or maybe "rgrep" for short. But I
./FAQ.md:1028:thought that was just as lame, and maybe a little too in-your-face. But I
./FAQ.md:1029:wanted to continue using `r` so I could at least pretend Rust had something to
./FAQ.md:1030:do with it.
./FAQ.md:1031:
./FAQ.md:1032:I spent a couple of days trying to think of very short words that began with
./FAQ.md:1033:the letter `r` that were even somewhat related to the task of searching. I
./FAQ.md:1034:don't remember how it popped into my head, but "rip" came up as something that
./FAQ.md:1035:meant "fast," as in, "to rip through your text." The fact that RIP is also
./FAQ.md:1036:an initialism for "Rest in Peace" (as in, "ripgrep kills grep") never really
./FAQ.md:1037:dawned on me. Perhaps the coincidence is too striking to believe that, but
./FAQ.md:1038:I didn't realize it until someone explicitly pointed it out to me after the
./FAQ.md:1039:initial public release. I admit that I found it mildly amusing, but if I had
./FAQ.md:1040:realized it myself before the public release, I probably would have pressed on
./FAQ.md:1041:and chose a different name. Alas, renaming things after a release is hard, so I
./FAQ.md:1042:decided to mush on.
./FAQ.md:1043:
./FAQ.md:1044:Given the fact that
./FAQ.md:1045:[ripgrep never was, is or will be a 100% drop-in replacement for
./FAQ.md:1046:grep](#posix4ever),
./FAQ.md:1047:ripgrep is neither actually a "grep killer" nor was it ever intended to be. It
./FAQ.md:1048:certainly does eat into some of its use cases, but that's nothing that other
./FAQ.md:1049:tools like ack or The Silver Searcher weren't already doing.
./FAQ.md:1050:
./FAQ.md:1051:
./FAQ.md:1052:<h3 name="donations">
./FAQ.md:1053:How can I donate to ripgrep or its maintainers?
./FAQ.md:1054:</h3>
./FAQ.md:1055:
./FAQ.md:1056:I welcome [sponsorship](https://github.com/sponsors/BurntSushi/).
./FAQ.md:1057:
./FAQ.md:1058:Or if you'd prefer, donating to a charitable organization that you like would
./FAQ.md:1059:also be most welcome. My favorites are:
./FAQ.md:1060:
./FAQ.md:1061:* [The Internet Archive](https://archive.org/donate/)

./GUIDE.md:1:## User Guide
./GUIDE.md:2:
./GUIDE.md:3:This guide is intended to give an elementary description of ripgrep and an
./GUIDE.md:4:overview of its capabilities. This guide assumes that ripgrep is
./GUIDE.md:5:[installed](README.md#installation)
./GUIDE.md:6:and that readers have passing familiarity with using command line tools. This
./GUIDE.md:7:also assumes a Unix-like system, although most commands are probably easily
./GUIDE.md:8:translatable to any command line shell environment.
./GUIDE.md:9:
